title: 03. Databases & Data Modeling: Column-Family Databases
summary: A column-family database is a NoSQL wide-column store that models data as a sorted, distributed, persistent, multi-dimensional map of (row_key, column_family, column_qualifier, timestamp) → value, exemplified by Google…
objectives: What is the difference between a partition key and a clustering key in Cassandra, and why does the distinction matter?
Explain the LSM-tree write path and why it makes column-family stores write-optimized.
What is a tombstone, and what happens if `gc_grace_seconds` is misconfigured?
Compare Size-Tiered (STCS), Leveled (LCS), and Time-Window (TWCS) compaction strategies.

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A **column-family database** is a NoSQL wide-column store that models data as a *sorted, distributed, persistent, multi-dimensional map* of `(row_key, column_family, column_qualifier, timestamp) → value`, exemplified by **Google Bigtable** (2006 paper), **Apache HBase**, and **Apache Cassandra** — where each row can have a different set of columns, rows are partitioned across nodes by row key, and within a partition rows are sorted by clustering keys, enabling both massive horizontal write scale and efficient range scans.

Column-family databases were born out of a frustration that relational databases could not scale to petabyte-class workloads like web crawl indexing, clickstream analytics, and time-ordered user activity. Google's 2006 Bigtable paper (Chang et al.) described a sparse, distributed, multi-dimensional sorted map — `(row:string, column:string, time:int64) → string`. The row key partitions data across tablet servers via range sharding; within a tablet, rows are kept sorted lexicographically by key, enabling fast prefix scans (e.g., "fetch all rows for user 42 in chronological order"). Columns are grouped into column families for storage and access-control locality, but each row may have any subset of columns — hence "sparse." Versions are tracked by timestamps, so the system naturally retains history and supports time-travel reads. Apache HBase is the open-source clone of Bigtable (runs on HDFS, strong consistency per row), and Apache Cassandra merged the Bigtable data model with Amazon Dynamo's distribution (consistent hashing, tunable consistency, masterless replication). Facebook built Cassandra for inbox search; Netflix adopted it aggressively for viewing history and the "continue watching" feature; Instagram uses Cassandra for feed and direct-message storage at multi-billion-user scale.

The data model can be visualized as a nested map: `Map<RowKey, SortedMap<ColumnFamily, SortedMap<ColumnQualifier, SortedMap<Timestamp, Value>>>>`. The **partition key** (a prefix of the row key in Cassandra) determines which node owns the row — in Cassandra this is computed via Murmur3 hash modulo the token ring, giving even distribution. The **clustering key** (the rest of the row key) determines sort order within a partition. For example, in `Netflix viewing history` modeled as `partition_key=user_id, clustering_key=(show_id, episode_id, watched_at)`, all of a user's viewing records live on one node, sorted so that "give me user 42's most recent 20 watches" is a single-disk sequential scan — no index hop, no network fan-out. This is the killer property: **data layout matches access pattern**. Writes are also fast because they append to an in-memory MemTable (a sorted structure) and sequentially to a CommitLog on disk — no random disk seeks, no B-tree rebalancing. Once the MemTable fills, it's flushed as an immutable SSTable (Sorted String Table) to disk.

The mechanical sympathy of LSM-trees (Log-Structured Merge-trees) is what makes wide-column stores write-optimized. A write goes: (1) append to CommitLog (sequential disk I/O, durable), (2) insert into MemTable (in-memory sorted structure). Both are O(1) amortized — no read-modify-write, no B-tree split. Reads, however, must consult MemTable, then potentially multiple SSTables on disk (each a sorted run), and merge them via a Bloom filter + MinIndex. This is why reads in Cassandra/HBase are typically slower than writes — but caching (row cache, key cache, chunk cache) mitigates hot reads. As SSTables accumulate, **compaction** merges them in the background to reclaim space and reduce read amplification. Three compaction strategies dominate: **Size-Tiered Compaction (STCS)** — merges SSTables of similar size, good for write-heavy workloads, but can leave many SSTables that reads must fan out to; **Leveled Compaction (LCS)** — maintains SSTables in levels where each level is 10× the previous, each level non-overlapping, dramatically reducing read amplification at the cost of higher write amplification; **Time-Window Compaction (TWCS)** — buckets SSTables by time window, ideal for time-series data where old data is rarely read.

Deletes are subtle. Wide-column stores never actually delete data immediately — they write a **tombstone**, a special marker that says "this column was deleted at timestamp T." Reads filter out anything ≤ the tombstone timestamp. Tombstones persist until compaction physically reclaims them (typically when all SSTables containing both the tombstone and the shadowed data are compacted together). This means deletions briefly increase disk usage, and if compaction falls behind, tombstones accumulate and reads slow (the database must scan past tombstones). The `gc_grace_seconds` setting (default 10 days in Cassandra) controls how long a tombstone must be retained before it can be dropped — long enough to ensure all replicas have seen it before any compaction resurrects shadowed data on a lagging replica. This is a critical operational gotcha: if a replica is down longer than `gc_grace_seconds` and the tombstone is compacted away elsewhere, that replica can resurrect deleted data on repair.

Real-world deployments illustrate the scale and patterns. **Netflix runs Cassandra** across 500+ nodes in 3 AWS regions (us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1) for viewing history, billing events, and the "continue watching" feature — multi-master active-active with LOCAL_QUORUM consistency, surviving full region loss without losing writes. **Instagram uses Cassandra** for feed storage (each user's feed is a partition keyed by user_id, with media_ids as clustering keys in reverse-chronological order) and for direct messages — billions of rows, sub-10ms reads. **Apple famously runs the largest known Cassandra cluster** (75,000+ nodes, tens of PB) for messages, photos, and device telemetry. **Twitter uses Cassandra** (and previously Rainbird) for analytics and feed. The common pattern: write-heavy, sparse-schema, time-series-ish workloads where the access pattern is "give me everything for this user/device/tenant in time order" — exactly what the wide-column layout optimizes for.

The trade-offs are real and explain why column-family stores aren't a default choice. First, **no joins** — relational queries must be denormalized at write time, often into materialized views (Cassandra Materialized Views are buggy and discouraged; better to maintain views application-side). Second, **limited secondary indexing** — Cassandra's SASI indexes are slow and discouraged at scale; you must design tables around queries (one table per access pattern, denormalized). Third, **no ad-hoc queries** — a query must specify the full partition key and (optionally) a contiguous range of clustering keys. "Find users in zip 94101" requires a separate table indexed by zip. Fourth, **operational complexity** — compaction tuning, tombstone management, repair operations (`nodetool repair`), JVM GC tuning, schema migrations — Cassandra/HBase clusters need dedicated SRE attention. Fifth, **eventual consistency by default** — Cassandra defaults to eventual consistency; strong consistency (LOCAL_QUORUM) adds latency, and serial consistency (LWT, Paxos-based) is 10× slower and discouraged for hot partitions. Sixth, **schema-rigid-but-sparse** — you must declare column families and types up front (Cassandra CQL), but each row may have any subset of columns, which is awkward to reason about. The takeaway: column-family databases are write-scaling champions for sparse, time-ordered, known-access-pattern data, but they demand up-front query design and dedicated operations.

(show_5, ep_3, ts=1.7B): {progress: 0.8}
(show_5, ep_4, ts=1.71B): {progress: 0.2}
(show_8, ep_1, ts=1.72B): {progress: 0.5}"] end Node -.-> DataModel ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` Column-family data model = sorted, distributed map of maps Map>> Netflix viewing-history example (Cassandra CQL): +------------+-------------+------------+------------+-----------+ | user_id | show_id | episode_id | watched_at | progress | | (PART KEY) | (CLUST KEY)| (CLUST KEY)| (CLUST KEY)| | +------------+-------------+------------+------------+-----------+ | user:42 | show:5 | ep:3 | 1.70B | 0.80 | | user:42 | show:5 | ep:4 | 1.71B | 0.20 | | user:42 | show:8 | ep:1 | 1.72B | 0.50 | | user:99 | show:2 | ep:1 | 1.70B | 1.00 | +------------+-------------+------------+------------+-----------+ Partition key -> Murmur3 hash -> token -> owns ONE node Clustering key -> sort order WITHIN partition (sequential disk scan) +-------------------+ +-------------------------+ | Write path | | Read path | +-------------------+ +-------------------------+ | 1. append WAL | | 1. check MemTable | | 2. insert MemTable| | 2. check Bloom filter | | 3. (async flush) | | 3. check SSTables (disk)| | -> SSTable | | 4. merge + filter | | O(1) amortized | | tombstones | +-------------------+ +-------------------------+ | v +--------------------------+ | Compaction strategies | +--------------------------+ | STCS size-tiered (W> R) | | LCS leveled (R > W) | | TWCS time-window (TS) | +--------------------------+ Tombstone lifecycle: DELETE row -> write tombstone marker (ts=T) Reads filter out shadowed data (ts <= T) Compaction reclaims space AFTER gc_grace_seconds (default 10d) ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The client issues a CQL statement `SELECT * FROM watch_history WHERE user_id = 42 AND watched_at > 1.7B`. The driver hashes the partition key `user_id=42` via Murmur3 modulo the token ring to determine the owning replica set (primary + 2 replicas in Cassandra RF=3). The coordinator node forwards the request to enough replicas to satisfy the requested consistency level (LOCAL_ONE, LOCAL_QUORUM, etc.). 2. On the owning node, the read consults the in-memory MemTable first (recent un-flushed writes), then the Bloom filter for each on-disk SSTable to skip ones that definitely don't contain the partition key, then the SSTable index to find the partition offset, then reads the partition blocks from disk. Multiple SSTable fragments are merged by timestamp, with tombstones filtering out shadowed data. 3. The clustering keys are already sorted within the partition, so the requested `watched_at > 1.7B` filter is a contiguous range scan — sequential disk reads, no random seeks. Compaction runs in the background to merge SSTables and reclaim tombstones once `gc_grace_seconds` has elapsed. Real-world: Netflix's viewing-history reads return the user's most recent 20 watches in single-digit milliseconds because the data layout matches the access pattern exactly.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Column-family store mock: partition key + clustering keys, MemTable + SSTable (sorted), tombstones, and time-window compaction (TWCS).
- Immutable, sorted on-disk table (here: in-memory list).
- Cassandra-style wide-column store with MemTable + SSTables.
- SELECT * WHERE pk=?
- Partition_key -> list of (clustering_tuple, ts, value_or_tombstone)
- Tombstone: value=None means "deleted at ts"
- Merge MemTable + all SSTables, latest ts wins, skip tombstoned
- Filter tombstones (val is None for the winning ts)

**Defines:** `SSTable`, `ColumnFamilyStore`

```python
"""
Column-family store mock: partition key + clustering keys, MemTable +
SSTable (sorted), tombstones, and time-window compaction (TWCS).

Demonstrates:
  - Wide-column data model: row key -> sorted columns
  - Partition routing (hash of partition key)
  - Clustering sort order within partition (range scan)
  - Tombstone writes on delete
  - TWCS-style compaction (drop old tombstones)

Models a simplified Cassandra-style single-node store.

Run:  python3 column_family.py
"""

import hashlib
import bisect
import time
from collections import defaultdict

class SSTable:
    """Immutable, sorted on-disk table (here: in-memory list)."""

    def __init__(self, rows_by_partition):
        # partition_key -> list of (clustering_tuple, ts, value_or_tombstone)
        self._data = {pk: sorted(rows) for pk, rows in rows_by_partition.items()}

    def get_partition(self, partition_key):
        return self._data.get(partition_key, [])

class ColumnFamilyStore:
    """Cassandra-style wide-column store with MemTable + SSTables."""

    def __init__(self, name, partition_key, clustering_keys):
        self.name = name
        self.partition_key = partition_key
        self.clustering_keys = clustering_keys
        self._memtable = defaultdict(list)   # pk -> list of (clust, ts, val)
        self._sstables = []                  # list of SSTable
        self._memtable_flush_at = 100        # rows

    # ----- internal helpers -----
    def _pk(self, row):
        return str(row[self.partition_key])

    def _clust(self, row):
        return tuple(row[c] for c in self.clustering_keys)

    def _flush_memtable(self):
        if not self._memtable:
            return
        self._sstables.append(SSTable(self._memtable))
        self._memtable = defaultdict(list)
        print(f"  [FLUSH] MemTable -> SSTable #{len(self._sstables)}")

    # ----- public API -----
    def insert(self, row, ts=None):
        ts = ts or int(time.time())
        pk, clust = self._pk(row), self._clust(row)
        self._memtable[pk].append((clust, ts, dict(row)))
        if sum(len(v) for v in self._memtable.values()) >= self._memtable_flush_at:
            self._flush_memtable()

    def delete(self, partition_key_value, clustering_values, ts=None):
        ts = ts or int(time.time())
        pk = str(partition_key_value)
        # Tombstone: value=None means "deleted at ts"
        self._memtable[pk].append((tuple(clustering_values), ts, None))

    def select(self, partition_key_value, clustering_range=None, limit=100):
        """SELECT * WHERE pk=? AND clust IN range LIMIT n."""
        pk = str(partition_key_value)
        # Merge MemTable + all SSTables, latest ts wins, skip tombstoned
        merged = defaultdict(dict)  # clust -> {ts: value}
        for source in [self._memtable] + [s._data for s in self._sstables]:
            for clust, ts, val in source.get(pk, []):
                if clust not in merged or ts >= max(merged[clust].keys()):
                    merged[clust] = {ts: val}
        # Filter tombstones (val is None for the winning ts)
        results = [(clust, ts, val) for clust, m in merged.items()
                   for ts, val in m.items() if val is not None]
        # Sort by clustering key (Cassandra clustering order)
        results.sort(key=lambda r: r[0])
        # Apply range filter on clustering keys
        if clustering_range:
            lo, hi = clustering_range
            results = [r for r in results if lo <= r[0] <= hi]
        return results[:limit]

    def compact_twcs(self, window_seconds):
        """Time-Window Compaction: drop tombstones older than window."""
        now = int(time.time())
        before = sum(len(s._data) for s in self._sstables)
        new_sstables = []
        for sst in self._sstables:
            kept = defaultdict(list)
            for pk, rows in sst._data.items():
                for clust, ts, val in rows:
                    if val is None and (now - ts) > window_seconds:
                        continue  # drop old tombstone
                    kept[pk].append((clust, ts, val))
            if kept:
                new_sstables.append(SSTable(kept))
        self._sstables = new_sstables
        print(f"  [TWCS] SSTables: {len(self._sstables)}; "
              f"compacted away old tombstones (window={window_seconds}s)")

# ---------------- demo ----------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    store = ColumnFamilyStore(
        name="watch_history",
        partition_key="user_id",
        clustering_keys=("show_id", "episode_id", "watched_at"),
    )

    print("=== Inserts (Netflix viewing history) ===")
    store.insert({"user_id": 42, "show_id": 5,  "episode_id": 3, "watched_at": 1_700_000_000, "progress": 0.8})
    store.insert({"user_id": 42, "show_id": 5,  "episode_id": 4, "watched_at": 1_700_000_500, "progress": 0.2})
    store.insert({"user_id": 42, "show_id": 8,  "episode_id": 1, "watched_at": 1_700_001_000, "progress": 0.5})
    store.insert({"user_id": 99, "show_id": 2,  "episode_id": 1, "watched_at": 1_700_000_000, "progress": 1.0})

    print("\n=== SELECT WHERE user_id=42 (range scan within partition) ===")
    for clust, ts, val in store.select(42):
        print(f"  {val}")

    print("\n=== DELETE user_id=42, show_id=5, episode_id=3 (tombstone) ===")
    store.delete(42, (5, 3, 1_700_000_000), ts=int(time.time()))

    print("\n=== SELECT after delete (tombstone filters shadowed data) ===")
    for clust, ts, val in store.select(42):
        print(f"  {val}")

    print("\n=== TWCS compaction (drops old tombstones) ===")
    store.compact_twcs(window_seconds=1)
    print("\n=== Final partition layout ===")
    print(f"  SSTables on disk: {len(store._sstables)}")
    print("  Wide-column trade-offs:")
    print("    + write-optimized (LSM: append WAL + MemTable, O(1) amortized)")
    print("    + clustering keys enable sequential range scans within partition")
    print("    + sparse rows (each row can have different columns)")
    print("    - no joins; one table per access pattern (denormalize)")
    print("    - tombstones must wait gc_grace_seconds before compaction GC")
    print("    - compaction tuning (STCS/LCS/TWCS) is operationally complex")
```

quiz.explanation: The partition key is hashed (Murmur3 in Cassandra) to determine which node in the cluster owns the row — it controls data placement and parallelism. All rows with the same partition key live on the same node (and its replicas), so cross-partition queries require multiple network hops. The clustering key determines the sort order of rows within a partition on disk — it controls range-scan efficiency.

quiz.explanation: tombstone** is a deletion marker — when you DELETE FROM table WHERE ..., Cassandra/HBase doesn't physically remove the data immediately; it writes a special marker saying "this column was deleted at timestamp T." Reads then filter out any version with timestamp ≤ T. This is necessary because data may exist in multiple immutable SSTables, and physical removal would require rewriting all of them.
